paragraphs.title: A Plea for God’s Intervention against the Enemies

easy.explanation: The psalm begins, “Keep not thou silence, O God.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask God not to do?

answers: God’s enemies and those who hate Him
easy.explanation: The verse says that God’s enemies have made a tumult and lifted up the head.
easy.q: Who has lifted up the head?

easy.explanation: They have taken crafty counsel against God’s people.
easy.q: Against whom have the enemies taken crafty counsel?

answers: The enemies are making a tumult and showing pride
The people are celebrating a victory
medium.explanation: The enemies are noisy and arrogant, so the psalmist asks God not to remain still.
medium.q: Why does the psalmist call on God to act?

medium.explanation: The phrase parallels “Keep not thou silence” and asks God to respond.
medium.q: In this context, what does “hold not thy peace” mean?

answers: A plea for action followed by a description of the enemies
A song of thanksgiving followed by a list of offerings
A military victory followed by a royal feast
medium.explanation: The psalmist first calls on God to act and then describes the enemies’ behavior.
medium.q: What is the movement of these verses?

answers: The urgent need for divine intervention
challenge.explanation: The repeated appeals emphasize the urgency of the situation and the need for God to act.
challenge.q: What is emphasized by the repeated appeals for God not to be silent or still?

challenge.explanation: In this setting, lifting up the head suggests pride and defiance.
challenge.q: How does “lifted up the head” characterize the enemies?

answers: They are His enemies and haters
challenge.explanation: They are explicitly called God’s enemies and those who hate Him.
challenge.q: What relationship to God do the enemies have in these verses?

easy.explanation: They have consulted against God’s hidden ones, meaning His protected people.
easy.q: Against whom have the enemies consulted?

answers: Cut Israel off as a nation
easy.explanation: They say, “let us cut them off from being a nation.”
easy.q: What do the enemies want to do to Israel?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “they are confederate against thee.”
easy.q: What have the enemies made against God?

answers: Their shared counsel leads them to unite
Their counsel causes them to retreat
There is no connection between them
medium.explanation: After consulting together, they join themselves in a common alliance.
medium.q: What is the connection between the enemies’ counsel and their confederacy?

answers: They have secretly planned a scheme
They have asked for wise instruction
medium.explanation: The word “crafty” indicates a concealed and deceitful plan.

answers: That Israel’s name should be remembered no more
That Israel should protect the enemies
medium.explanation: They want Israel to be cut off so that its name will no longer be remembered.
medium.q: What is the stated purpose of the enemies’ plan?

answers: It stresses the enemies’ unity and coordination
It shows that they are divided
It shows that they have abandoned their plan
challenge.explanation: The phrase indicates that the enemies are acting together with a common purpose.
challenge.q: Why is the phrase “with one consent” important?

answers: The plot is directed both against God’s people and against God Himself
The plot concerns only foreign kings
The enemies have no interest in Israel
challenge.explanation: The passage presents an attack on God’s people as an opposition to God Himself.
challenge.q: What is shown by the movement from “thy people” to “against thee”?

answers: Secret counsel, a plan to erase Israel, and an alliance against God
A surrender, a feast, and a song of praise
A journey, a sacrifice, and a royal coronation
challenge.explanation: The enemies plan secretly, seek to erase Israel, and unite against God.

paragraphs.title: The Coalition of Nations against Israel

answers: A list of peoples and forces joining the conflict
easy.explanation: The verses name the various peoples and groups involved in the coalition.
easy.q: What do these verses mainly provide?

easy.explanation: Moab is listed among the peoples joining the coalition.
easy.q: Which people are named in the passage?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “Assur also is joined with them.”
easy.q: Who is said to be joined with the other nations?

medium.explanation: Moab, Ammon, and Amalek all appear in the list.
medium.q: Which group contains only peoples named in verses 7–9?

medium.explanation: The phrase states that Assur became part of the group.
medium.q: What does “is joined with them” mean?

answers: It emphasizes the size of the coalition
It shows that there is only one enemy
It describes their ordinary daily life
medium.explanation: The long list highlights the broad alliance gathered against God’s people.
medium.q: What is the main effect of listing so many peoples?

answers: The repeated naming of many peoples and territories
The use of the word “also” alone
challenge.explanation: The number of named groups makes the coalition appear extensive.
challenge.q: Which detail most strongly conveys the breadth of the coalition?

answers: Assur served as a supporting power for them
Assur fought against every other nation
The children of Lot defended Israel
challenge.explanation: To help the children of Lot means Assur acted as a supporting force for them.
challenge.q: What does the statement that Assur helped the children of Lot imply?

answers: The passage moves from the plot to a list of its participants
The passage moves from victory to thanksgiving
The passage moves from peace to rest
challenge.explanation: After describing the conspiracy, the psalm names the peoples involved in it.
challenge.q: What organizing principle governs these verses?

paragraphs.title: A Plea for Victory Like Earlier Defeats

easy.explanation: The psalmist asks God to act as He did against the Midianites, Sisera, and Jabin.
easy.q: Which earlier enemies does the psalmist mention as examples?

answers: They perished and became dung for the earth
easy.explanation: The verse says they perished at Endor and became as dung for the earth.
easy.q: What happened to the enemies at Endor?

answers: Make them like the defeated leaders Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah, and Zalmunna
easy.explanation: The psalmist asks that their nobles and princes suffer the fate of those earlier leaders.
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask God to do to the enemy leaders?

answers: To ask for a similar victory over the present enemies
To conceal the identity of the nations
medium.explanation: Earlier victories serve as examples of what the psalmist asks God to do again.
medium.q: Why does the psalmist recall earlier defeats?

medium.explanation: The following phrase identifies them as princes, or rulers.
medium.q: What does “nobles” mean in this context?

answers: Earlier defeats, the destruction of enemies, and judgment on their leaders
A list of nations, a covenant, and thanksgiving
A storm, a search for God’s name, and a title
medium.explanation: The verses recall past defeats and ask that the current enemies and their leaders be similarly overthrown.

answers: They serve as examples of victories God had already given
They are presented as the current allies of Israel
They prove that the enemies have won
challenge.explanation: Their defeat provides a pattern for the victory the psalmist requests.
challenge.q: What role do the Midianites, Sisera, and Jabin play in the psalmist’s argument?

answers: Both illustrate complete judgment on God’s enemies
They describe peace between the nations
challenge.explanation: The passage presents both the destruction of the forces and the downfall of their leaders.
challenge.q: How are the defeat at Endor and the judgment of the leaders related?

answers: The request includes the power directing the coalition
The leaders are being offered protection
challenge.explanation: The psalmist asks that the rulers who guide the opposition also be judged.
challenge.q: What is implied by mentioning the leaders along with the armies?

paragraphs.title: The Destruction and Scattering of the Enemies

easy.explanation: The psalmist asks God to make them like stubble before the wind.
easy.q: What image is used for the enemies’ scattering?

easy.explanation: The verses use images of fire, wind, tempest, and storm.
easy.q: Which forces of nature are mentioned?

easy.explanation: The psalmist says, “persecute them with thy tempest, and make them afraid with thy storm.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask God to do with the enemies through the storm?

answers: It can be easily blown away by the wind
It becomes heavier in the wind
medium.explanation: Stubble is light and easily scattered, portraying the enemies as unable to stand.
medium.q: Why is stubble an effective image for the enemies?

medium.explanation: The storm is portrayed as producing fear and confusion among the enemies.
medium.q: What does “make them afraid” mean in the setting of the storm?

answers: It moves from burning and scattering to pursuit and terror
It moves from rest to peace and blessing
It moves from building to planting and guarding
medium.explanation: The images progress through fire, wind, tempest, pursuit, and fear.
medium.q: How does the description of divine action develop?

answers: They suggest powerful forces that consume and disperse
They portray the enemies as secure rulers
challenge.explanation: Fire consumes and wind scatters, making them fitting images of decisive divine action.
challenge.q: Why do fire and wind suit the psalmist’s request?

answers: The sense of overwhelming power against the enemies
The sense that the danger has ended
challenge.explanation: The successive images intensify the picture of divine judgment.
challenge.q: What is strengthened by the movement from stubble to fire and storm?

answers: Their unity and ability to act together are destroyed
challenge.explanation: Scattering reverses the united coalition described earlier in the psalm.
challenge.q: What result is implied by scattering the enemies like stubble?

paragraphs.title: The Enemies’ Shame and Recognition of the Lord’s Supremacy

easy.explanation: The verse says, “Fill their faces with shame.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask God to fill the enemies’ faces with?

easy.explanation: The purpose stated is “that they may seek thy name, O LORD.”
easy.q: What may the enemies seek after being covered with shame?

answers: That Jehovah alone is most high over all the earth
That the enemies rule the earth
easy.explanation: The final verse declares that Jehovah alone is the most high over all the earth.
easy.q: What should people know at the end of the psalm?

answers: Shame is intended to lead the enemies to seek God’s name
Shame causes them to proclaim their own victory
medium.explanation: The psalmist asks for shame so that the enemies may seek the Lord’s name.
medium.q: What connection does the passage make between shame and seeking God’s name?

medium.explanation: Alongside being troubled and put to shame, “confounded” describes disgrace and confusion.
medium.q: In this context, what does “confounded” mean?

answers: Shame, confusion, and destruction leading to recognition of God’s supremacy
medium.explanation: The requested judgment leads ultimately to recognition that Jehovah alone is supreme.
medium.q: What is the progression in verses 17–19?

answers: That people may know Jehovah’s unique supremacy
That the enemies may form a stronger alliance
That Israel’s name may be erased
challenge.explanation: The final purpose is that people may know Jehovah is the most high over all the earth.
challenge.q: What deeper purpose is given for the judgment at the end of the psalm?

answers: The opening asks God to act, and the ending describes the recognition of His power
The opening and ending both only list nations
The ending cancels the request for divine intervention
challenge.explanation: The psalm moves from asking God not to remain silent to proclaiming the result of His action.
challenge.q: How does the ending relate to the opening request?

answers: The uniqueness and exclusivity of the Lord’s supremacy
The existence of many equal gods
challenge.explanation: The word “alone” stresses that Jehovah uniquely holds supreme authority over all the earth.
challenge.q: What does “whose name alone is JEHOVAH” emphasize?
